column1: What is the core invariant governing lottery probability calculations under fair draw mechanics?
column2: The principle of equally likely outcomes: every valid combination occupies the same probability mass in the sample space, so probability of any specific outcome = 1 / total number of possible outcomes.

column1: When should permutations vs. combinations be used in lottery probability calculations?
column2: Use permutations when order matters; use combinations when order does not matter. Most lottery number selections use combinations since matching numbers in any order wins.

column1: How does sampling without replacement differ from sampling with replacement in lottery mechanics?
column2: Without replacement: each draw removes an element, shrinking the denominator and creating dependence between draws (standard in most government lotteries). With replacement: population size stays constant, producing independent events whose joint probability is a simple product.

column1: What is the formula for the probability of winning the jackpot in a 6/49 lottery?
What jackpot-to-ticket-price ratio makes a 6/49 lottery actuarially fair (ignoring lower prize tiers)?
column2: The jackpot must equal exactly 13,983,816 times the ticket price (the reciprocal of the win probability) for expected value to equal zero.

column1: Define 'expected value' in the context of a lottery ticket.
column2: E[X] = Σ (probability of each outcome × net payoff of that outcome), i.e., the probability-weighted average of all possible prize payoffs minus the ticket price.

column1: What is the 'take-out rate' in lottery economics?
column2: The fraction of gross ticket sales that the lottery operator retains before distributing prizes, typically 40-50% for traditional number-draw lotteries. It sets an upper bound on possible expected value for players.

column1: Why can expected value never exceed the pool percentage in a lottery with a given take-out rate?
column2: Because only the complement of the take-out rate (e.g., 50-60 cents per dollar wagered) is returned to the prize pool; aggregate expected return across all ticket purchasers cannot exceed this pooled percentage, regardless of jackpot size.

column1: What makes a lottery ticket a 'negative expected value proposition'?
column2: When the sum of probability-weighted payoffs falls below the ticket price, meaning the expected net return is negative — true for virtually all operating lotteries after operator take and taxes.

column1: What distribution models probability for lottery draws without replacement, and what models unique combination counts?
column2: The hypergeometric distribution models probabilities for drawing without replacement; the multinomial coefficient (combinations formula) calculates unique combination counts.

column1: What three practitioner objectives define the operational lottery mathematics labs?
column2: 1) Construct expected value and variance decompositions for multi-tier payouts via combinatorial probability; 2) Reverse-engineer the revenue extraction model via payout ratios and rollover mechanics; 3) Empirically test behavioral mispricing of low-probability high-payoff events via willingness-to-pay experiments.

column1: What behavioral finance phenomenon explains why rational individuals still buy lottery tickets despite negative expected value?
column2: Systematic deviations from expected utility maximization — individuals misperceive/overweight small probabilities of large payoffs, a bias captured by extensions like prospect theory rather than classical expected value calculations.
